share.who: a backend developer whose fixed-window limiter allowed a burst
share.why: 20 requests in 2 seconds can pass a limit of 10 per 10 seconds: worth sending to whoever wrote the limiter

replay.twist: On a second watch '1 Redis script, 1 formula, 1 HTTP header' in the hook reads as the checklist the video just walked through: the script (Lua EVAL), the formula (49.5 requests) and the header (Retry-After).

length_reason: About 118 s on purpose: a technical deep dive with a real artefact in every part (redis-cli INCR, a crash between INCR and EXPIRE, the Lua script, the fixed-window edge, the sliding window counter formula, PTTL and the 429 with Retry-After, the token bucket, Stripe's other limiters).

claims.say: A rate limiter stops a client from sending too many requests in a given amount of time.
claims.quote: The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ("rate limiting").

claims.say: The 429 mechanism of asking the client to slow down is commonly called rate limiting.
claims.quote: The HTTP 429 Too Many Requests client error response status code indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. This mechanism of asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called "rate limiting".

claims.say: The key includes the window number, so a new window starts a fresh count.
claims.quote: The counter key includes the window number, so a new window automatically starts a fresh count.

claims.say: INCR creates the key at 1 if it does not exist, otherwise it increments (example output (integer) 1).
claims.quote: INCR creates or increments. If the key doesn't exist, INCR creates it at 1. Otherwise it increments.

claims.say: EXPIRE is set when count == 1, the first request in a new window.
claims.quote: Expiry on first request. When count == 1 this is the first request in a new window. The script sets EXPIRE so the key auto-deletes after the window passes.

claims.say: A client could send 10 requests at second 9 and 10 more at second 11: 20 requests in 2 seconds within a limit of 10 per 10 seconds.
claims.quote: A client could send 10 requests at second 9 and another 10 at second 11 — 20 requests in 2 seconds while technically staying within a "10 per 10 seconds" limit, because the requests straddle two windows.

claims.say: Cloudflare's previous-counter estimate uses the previous window's counter to extrapolate the request rate.
claims.quote: But actually, can't we just use the information from the previous counter in order to extrapolate an accurate approximation of the request rate?

claims.say: Worked example: limit 50 requests per minute, 18 requests in the current minute that started 15 seconds ago, 42 in the previous minute: rate = 42 * ((60-15)/60) + 18 = 42 * 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 requests.
claims.quote: Let's say I set a limit of 50 requests per minute on an API endpoint. In this situation, I did 18 requests during the current minute, which started 15 seconds ago, and 42 requests during the entire previous minute. rate = 42 * ((60-15)/60) + 18 = 42 * 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 requests

claims.say: The previous-counter estimate is an approximation.
claims.quote: This algorithm assumes a constant rate of requests during the previous sampling period (which can be any time span), this is why the result is only an approximation of the actual rate.

claims.say: In Cloudflare's analysis of 400 million requests, 0.003% were wrongly allowed or rate limited.
claims.quote: It is still very accurate, as an analysis on 400 million requests from 270,000 distinct sources shown: 0.003% of requests have been wrongly allowed or rate limited

claims.say: A blocked client gets HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.
claims.quote: The HTTP 429 Too Many Requests client error response status code indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.

claims.say: The response may include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.
claims.quote: The response representations SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.

claims.say: Example response: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests, Content-Type: text/html, Retry-After: 3600.
claims.quote: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Content-Type: text/html Retry-After: 3600

claims.say: Retry-After holds either a number of seconds to wait or a date after which to retry.
claims.quote: <http-date>: A date after which to retry. <delay-seconds>: A non-negative decimal integer indicating the seconds to delay after the response is received.

claims.say: Retry-After example lines: Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT and Retry-After: 120.
claims.quote: Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT Retry-After: 120

claims.say: Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm: each user has a bucket, each request removes a token, more tokens slowly drip in, an empty bucket rejects the request.
claims.quote: We use the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting. This algorithm has a centralized bucket host where you take tokens on each request, and slowly drip more tokens into the bucket. If the bucket is empty, reject the request. In our case, every Stripe user has a bucket, and every time they make a request we remove a token from that bucket.

claims.say: Stripe's request rate limiter restricts each user to N requests per second.
claims.quote: This rate limiter restricts each user to N requests per second.

claims.say: Stripe also runs a concurrent requests limiter, for example 20 API requests in progress at the same time.
claims.quote: Instead of "You can use our API 1000 times a second", this rate limiter says "You can only have 20 API requests in progress at the same time".

claims.say: Load shedders make decisions based on the whole state of the system.
claims.quote: A load shedder makes its decisions based on the whole state of the system rather than the user who is making the request.

claims.say: Fixed window and sliding window are rate limiter algorithms (the Redis tutorial builds rate limiters with these).
claims.quote: Build 5 Rate Limiters with Redis: Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket, and Leaky Bucket

claims.say: The 429 example response is the one in RFC 6585.
claims.quote: RFC 6585 Additional HTTP Status Codes

claims.say: A Redis fixed-window limiter keeps one string key per window and bumps it with INCR.
claims.quote: STRING — one key per window, using INCR to bump the count and EXPIRE to auto-clean the key. A Lua script wraps both commands into a single atomic EVAL call.

claims.say: A fixed window rate limiter counts requests within discrete time intervals.
claims.quote: A fixed window rate limiter counts requests within discrete, non-overlapping time intervals. It is the simplest Redis rate limiting algorithm.

claims.say: INCR gives each concurrent caller a unique, sequential count.
claims.quote: INCR creates or increments. If the key doesn't exist, INCR creates it at 1. Otherwise it increments. Each concurrent caller gets a unique, sequential count.

claims.say: A crash between 2 Redis commands (INCR and EXPIRE) can leave a key with no expiry, so it is never auto-cleaned (keys leak).
claims.quote: STRING — one key per window, using INCR to bump the count and EXPIRE to auto-clean the key. ... Without this, a crash between the two commands could leave a key with no expiry

claims.say: So run INCR and EXPIRE in one Lua script with EVAL; Redis executes Lua scripts atomically.
claims.quote: The entire increment-and-expire sequence runs inside a single EVAL call. Redis executes Lua scripts atomically, so no other command can interleave between the INCR and the EXPIRE.

claims.say: Lua scripts call Redis commands with redis.call(); keys arrive in KEYS and other arguments in ARGV (example script uses redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) and redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])).
claims.quote: It is possible to call Redis commands from a Lua script either via redis.call() or redis.pcall(). The execution context makes arguments available to the script through KEYS and ARGV global runtime variables. > EVAL "return redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])" 1 foo bar

claims.say: A sliding window counter blends two fixed-window counters (uses the previous counter) to approximate a sliding window.
claims.quote: A sliding window counter rate limiter blends two fixed-window counters using a weighted average to approximate a true sliding window.

claims.say: Cloudflare uses the previous counter to approximate the rate (sliding windows).
claims.quote: Sliding windows to the rescue. But actually, can't we just use the information from the previous counter in order to extrapolate an accurate approximation of the request rate?

claims.say: Retry-After here comes from the key's remaining time to live (PTTL, in milliseconds; example value 6500 ms rounds up to 7 s).
claims.quote: PTTL for retry-after. The script also fetches the key's remaining TTL in milliseconds.
